source: Simon (1973) The structure of ill structured problems
finding: Simon defines an ill-structured problem (ISP) as a residual category: anything that is not a well-structured problem (WSP). He lists six criteria for a WSP and argues the boundary is vague and has no formal definition.
numbers: Six WSP criteria: (1) definite test of any proposed solution, mechanizable; (2) a problem space holding initial, goal and all reachable states; (3) legal moves as state transitions; (4) all acquirable knowledge representable in the space; (5) state changes mirror the real-world laws exactly; (6) all of this needs only practicable computation.
quote: ill structured problem (ISP) is a residual concept.
limits: Conceptual paper, no experiment. Criteria are relative to the power of the solver, so the line moves with the solver.
agent_relevance: Our agent should not treat 'ill-structured' as a fixed class. The same task is more or less ill-structured depending on tools and checks available. S6 search is the way to add structure.

source: Simon (1973) The structure of ill structured problems
finding: Core thesis: there is no real boundary between WSPs and ISPs, and no new type of problem-solving process is needed for ISPs. Ordinary GPS-style search plus retrieval is enough.
numbers: Abstract: any process looks ill-structured if the solver is a serial machine with a very large long-term memory or a very large external memory giving real-world consequences.
quote: no reason to suppose that new and hitherto unknown concepts or techniques are needed
limits: Thesis is argued, not tested. Written in 1973 before LLMs; it assumes a serial symbolic processor.
agent_relevance: Supports a single-scaffold design: no separate 'creative mode' for open problems. The same state machine plus operators can handle both. Matches schema section 4b (do not add new modes).

source: Simon (1973) The structure of ill structured problems
finding: Even theorem proving and chess are not truly well-structured. The solver may want to consider moves that are not 'legal', or use metalanguage, analogy or models from another space. If new resources may 'occur' during solving, the problem counts as ill-structured. Chess is a WSP in the small and an ISP in the large, because a real move is irrevocable and redefines the problem.
numbers: Examples: theorem proving (conditions 2-4 violated by considerable-but-illegal moves and meta knowledge); chess (conditions 1 and 5 violated over a full game).
quote: well structured in the small, but ill structured in the large
limits: Argument by example, no data.
agent_relevance: Local well-structured sub-problems inside a globally open task is where code-checkable steps (G2, G3) can be placed. Check at the small scale, plan at the large scale.

source: Simon (1973) The structure of ill structured problems
finding: Simon claims there are no WSPs, only ISPs that have been formalized for problem solvers, and that much problem-solving effort goes into structuring the problem, only a fraction into solving it once structured. He rebuts the strong form with Newell and Simon's point: if structuring were the whole of the work, only the first task in a series would be a problem.
numbers: Cites Newell and Simon 1972 p. 850 footnote 20.
quote: there are no WSPs. only ISPs that have been formalized for problem solvers.
limits: The rebuttal is logical, not empirical.
agent_relevance: Restating and structuring the problem is real work but not the only work. Budget both.

source: Simon (1973) The structure of ill structured problems
finding: The architect model: a design starts with a few open constraints (Reitman's fugue analysis). The task evokes from long-term memory attributes, sub-goals, requirements and alternative generators. The whole decomposes ('house' to 'floor plan plus structure', and so on). At any moment the architect works on a locally well-structured sub-problem, while a recognition and evoking mechanism keeps changing the problem space (Fig. 1: a GPS-like solver alternating with retrieval).
numbers: Fig. 1 parts: problem solver, immediate problem space (goals, constraints, specifications, alternative generators), long-term memory, external environment, evoking and noticing mechanism. Client budget is multiplied by 1.5 or 2 before the architect accepts it as a constraint.
limits: Descriptive model from Reitman's single protocol and Simon's own analysis. No quantitative fit.
agent_relevance: This is the earliest blueprint of our loop: a search core plus a retrieval step that adds constraints and sub-goals when something is noticed. Our S6 operators are generators evoked on impasse.

source: Simon (1973) The structure of ill structured problems
finding: Predicted failure modes of design by local sub-problems: interactions between sub-solutions are neglected; earlier solutions get undone when new aspects are attended to; criteria that were never evoked stay dormant; the final design depends on the ORDER of steps (facade first versus floor plan first gives different designs).
numbers: Qualitative. Mitigations named: divide the task into near self-contained components; set global parameters early (such as style) as constraints; ship design uses round-table conferences to resolve overlap among about 14 departments.
quote: the final product may be very much influenced by the order in which the design steps are taken up.
limits: Predictions, not tested in this paper.
agent_relevance: Matches known LLM issues: later edits break earlier constraints. Argues for a persistent constraint ledger checked by code at the end (G3, G2) and for order-sensitivity tests: run two orderings and compare.

source: Simon (1973) The structure of ill structured problems
finding: Why ISPs look ill-structured: the solver is serial and its long-term memory is large, so most memory is irrelevant over any short interval and must be evoked on recognition. The apparent changing of the problem space is retrieval, not a new kind of reasoning. Information enters by three channels: long-term memory, instructions, and the external world. Assimilation also conserves existing formulations: the solver sees the world through its preconceptions.
numbers: Memory search is said to be several orders of magnitude easier than perception because the designer controls the format. Hayes and Simon built a program that turns simple natural-language instructions into GPS input.
quote: The world as perceived is better structured than the raw world outside.
limits: Claims about future AI (1973) were optimistic; the paper has no performance data.
agent_relevance: LLMs invert this: memory is huge and retrieval is automatic, but the model is strongly bound to its first framing. Reframing should be triggered by code on a failed check (G1), not by schedule.

source: Newell and Simon (1972) Human Problem Solving
finding: Founding statement of problem-space theory: a problem solver holds a task environment, builds a problem space (states, operators, goal test) and searches it using heuristics such as means-ends analysis (GPS). Evidence came from think-aloud protocols on cryptarithmetic, logic and chess. Problem solving is selective search in a space whose size is controlled by heuristics.
numbers: Not verified this session. I did not read the text and give no figures.
limits: Book not opened; known only through Simon 1973 and Yao et al. (2023) which cite it. Later work questioned that a single fixed space explains human behaviour.
agent_relevance: Direct ancestor of S6: the program expands a tree, tests nodes, prunes. Tree of Thoughts (a13) says explicitly it follows this line.

source: Reitman (1964/1965) Heuristic decision procedures, open constraints, and the structure of ill-defined problems; Cognition and Thought
finding: First extensive treatment of ill-defined problems. Reitman analysed a thinking-aloud protocol of a composer writing a fugue. Few constraints are given and some are open (incompletely specified). Further constraints are generated from one transformation of the problem to the next.
numbers: One composer protocol, as described by Simon 1973 p. 189. Reitman, as quoted by Simon: the main initial constraint is that the end product be a fugue.
limits: Secondary evidence only: read through Simon 1973. N=1 protocol. Not opened directly.
agent_relevance: Open constraints are a design pattern: keep an explicit list of constraints, mark which are open, and let code add new ones as they are discovered.

source: Rittel and Webber (1973) Dilemmas in a general theory of planning
finding: Wicked problems versus tame problems of science. Ten properties, including: no definitive formulation, no stopping rule, solutions are good or bad not true or false, no immediate or ultimate test, every attempt counts (one-shot), no enumerable set of solutions, each problem is unique and a symptom of another problem, and the choice of explanation determines the solution.
numbers: The PDF I fetched was a scanned image with no text layer, so I could not read it. The list is from background knowledge and a secondary summary; wording not verified.
limits: Not opened. Conceptual analysis, no empirical test. Simon (1973) argues the same problems are only ISPs, not a different kind.
agent_relevance: Two useful points: no stopping rule (we need a budget rule, G7) and no test (we need G3 held-out checks or must say no verdict is possible). Where no check exists, the agent must say so rather than fake one.

source: Goel and Pirolli (1992) The structure of design problem spaces
finding: Design problem space hypothesis: design problem spaces share invariant features across design tasks and differ from non-design problem spaces. They derived 12 invariants from information-processing theory and tested them on protocols from several design domains.
numbers: Only the abstract-level facts (12 invariants; design versus non-design hypothesis) from a search snippet. Full text blocked (403), so no sample sizes or percentages recorded.
limits: Not opened. Small number of protocols. Later work (Dorst and Cross 2001) refined the problem and solution picture.
agent_relevance: Design search differs from puzzle search: the agent must build and revise the space, not only walk it. Argues for operators that change the problem (reframe, relax a constraint) in S6, not only operators that extend a solution.

source: Dorst and Cross (2001) Creativity in the design process: co-evolution of problem-solution
finding: Protocol study of nine experienced industrial designers. Problem and solution spaces evolve together; a creative event is a bridge that pairs a problem framing with a partial solution. They add default and surprise problem and solution spaces.
numbers: N = 9 experienced industrial designers (from the abstract as returned by search). No further numbers recorded.
limits: Not opened. Small sample, one design task type, observational.
agent_relevance: Supports letting S6 operators alter the problem framing and the candidate solution together, then testing the pair. A single reframing pass followed by solution is the failure mode.

source: Yao et al. (2023) Tree of Thoughts: Deliberate Problem Solving with Large Language Models
finding: ToT frames LLM problem solving as search over a tree of thoughts, explicitly following Newell, Shaw and Simon (problem solving as search through a combinatorial problem space). It uses thought generation (sample or propose), a state evaluator (value or vote), and BFS or DFS with backtracking. Game of 24: success rises from 4% (CoT) to 74% (ToT b=5).
numbers: Game of 24, GPT-4, 100 hard games (indices 901-1000 of 1,362 from 4nums.com). IO 7.3%; CoT 4.0%; CoT-SC (k=100) 9.0%; ToT b=1 45%; ToT b=5 74%; IO+refine (k=10) 27%; IO best of 100 33%; CoT best of 100 49%.
quote: our method achieved a success rate of 74%
limits: One model (GPT-4), May 2023. The evaluator is the same model. Game of 24 has a crisp verifier. Cost is much higher than CoT. The refine baseline used ground-truth feedback.
agent_relevance: This is the S6 tree in the schema. The gain needs a cheap state evaluator; here the model also grades its own partial states.

source: Yao et al. (2023) Tree of Thoughts: Deliberate Problem Solving with Large Language Models
finding: Error analysis for Game of 24: about 60% of CoT samples already failed after the first step, i.e. the first three words (such as '4 + 9'). Left-to-right decoding commits early with no way to back out.
numbers: About 60% of CoT samples failed at step 1 of 3. Best-of-100 CoT reaches 49% but is still below ToT with b>1 at similar node counts.
quote: around 60% of CoT samples already failed the task after generating the first step
limits: Read from the figure text and prose; single task.
agent_relevance: Early commitment is the weak point. Branching at the first decision, with code-side pruning, targets where failure actually happens.

source: Yao et al. (2023) Tree of Thoughts: Deliberate Problem Solving with Large Language Models
finding: Mini crosswords (5x5, 20 games). ToT with DFS and pruning beats IO and CoT by a wide margin, and removing backtracking hurts. Pruning with a model evaluator is imperfect: it sometimes marks correct words impossible.
numbers: Success (letter %, word %, games solved): IO 38.7 / 14 / 0; CoT 40.6 / 15.6 / 1%; ToT 78 / 60 / 20% (4 of 20 games); ToT with oracle best state 82.4 / 67.5 / 35% (7 of 20); no pruning 65.4 / 41.5 / 5% (1 of 20); no backtracking 54.6 / 20 / 5%. DFS limited to 100 steps.
limits: Only 20 games. The oracle best-state result shows the output heuristic loses 3 solved games.
agent_relevance: Backtracking matters (word-level 60% to 20% when removed). Pruning with a weak evaluator throws away correct branches: log pruned nodes or keep the evaluator conservative.

source: Yao et al. (2023) Tree of Thoughts: Deliberate Problem Solving with Large Language Models
finding: Creative writing (4 given sentences must end 4 paragraphs). ToT (plan then passage, 5 samples, vote, b=1) is judged more coherent than IO or CoT, by GPT-4 scores and by author comparison.
numbers: GPT-4 coherence score (1-10): IO 6.19, CoT 6.93, ToT 7.56. Authors prefer ToT over CoT in 41 of 100 pairs, CoT over ToT in 21, 38 similar. Iterative refine raises IO 6.19 to 7.67 and ToT 7.56 to 7.91. Score SD about 0.56. N = 100 inputs.
limits: The judge is GPT-4 itself and the human raters were a subset of the authors. Coherence is the only measure, not novelty. Conflicts with our G5 and G8 caution on model judges.
agent_relevance: An open-ended task gains from plan-level branching, but the evidence is a model-graded metric. Treat it as weak support for ill-structured creative work.

source: Valmeekam et al. (2023) On the planning abilities of large language models (a critical investigation)
finding: LLMs generate executable plans poorly on IPC-style domains. Average success about 3% in autonomous mode. Mystery Blocksworld (obfuscated names) is near 0, which suggests retrieval of known patterns, not planning. A human baseline shows the tasks are easy for people.
numbers: Blocksworld, 600 instances: plan generation GPT-3 6/600 (1%), Instruct-GPT3 41/600 (6.8%), BLOOM 4/250 (1.6%). Optimal planning 2/600, 35/600, 3/150. Mystery Blocksworld: GPT-3 0/600, Instruct-GPT3 7/600 (1.1%) for plan generation. Human study: 39 of 50 participants (78%) gave a valid plan; 35 of those 39 (89.7%) gave an optimal plan.
limits: Old models (GPT-3, Instruct-GPT3, BLOOM) from 2022. Blocksworld is a fully well-structured problem by Simon's criteria, so this tests search under complete rules, not ill-structured design.
agent_relevance: Even with fully stated rules, bare LLMs fail; the code-side search and verification in the schema add value before ill-structuredness is even considered. Disguised versions test for retrieval versus search.

source: Valmeekam et al. (2023) PlanBench: an extensible benchmark for evaluating LLMs on planning and reasoning about change
finding: A benchmark of IPC-style domains with test cases for plan generation, cost-optimal planning, verification, replanning, reuse and others. GPT-4 is better than Instruct-GPT3 but still fails most Blocksworld cases.
numbers: Blocksworld, 600 instances: GPT-4 plan generation 206/600 (34.3%) vs Instruct-GPT3 41/600 (6.8%); cost-optimal planning 198/600 (33%) vs 35/600 (5.8%); an auxiliary test 352/600 (58.6%) vs 72/600 (12%).
limits: Zero or one-shot prompting with early-2023 GPT-4. Only Blocksworld in the main table. Not tested on reasoning models.
agent_relevance: Gives a clean baseline for any test of the scaffold on well-structured search; the same instances can be run with and without our S6.

source: Hao et al. (2023) Reasoning with Language Model is Planning with World Model (RAP)
finding: RAP uses the LLM as both world model (predicts the next state) and reasoning agent, with Monte Carlo tree search guided by rewards. On Blocksworld a 33B LLaMA with RAP beats GPT-4 with CoT.
numbers: Blocksworld success by plan length (2/4/6-step): CoT LLaMA-33B 0.17 / 0.02 / 0.00; CoT pass@10 0.23 / 0.07 / 0.00; CoT GPT-4 0.50 / 0.63 / 0.40; RAP(10) 1.00 / 0.86 / 0.26; RAP(20) 1.00 / 0.88 / 0.42. Average RAP success 64%. GSM8k: RAP 48.8%.
limits: LLaMA-33B era. RAP(10) is below GPT-4 CoT at 6 steps. Compute is 10 to 20 MCTS iterations per problem. Rewards come from model self-evaluation.
agent_relevance: State-space search with a world model lifts a small model above a large one on search-heavy tasks. Supports spending tokens on S6 search rather than a bigger model; count cost per problem (G7).

source: Zhou et al. (2023/24) Language Agent Tree Search (LATS)
finding: LATS puts MCTS around LLM reasoning, acting and reflection, with an LLM value function and self-reflection on failed branches. It tops several baselines on HotpotQA and programming.
numbers: HotpotQA EM (GPT-3.5, reasoning): CoT 0.34, CoT-SC 0.38, ToT 0.55, RAP 0.60, LATS (CoT) 0.62. Acting: ReAct 0.32, Reflexion 0.51, ToT(ReAct) 0.39, RAP(ReAct) 0.54, LATS(ReAct) 0.63, LATS n=10 0.65, LATS(CoT+ReAct) 0.71. HumanEval Pass@1 GPT-3.5: LATS 83.8 vs Reflexion 68.1, ToT 54.4, RAP 63.1. GPT-4: LATS 92.7 vs Reflexion 91.0, base 80.1.
limits: Test-time compute is much larger than the baselines, so budgets are not equal. HumanEval has unit tests as an external signal. The gain over Reflexion on GPT-4 is 1.7 points.
agent_relevance: Search plus reflection beats single-pass at a higher budget. Not an equal-token comparison, so G7 is not settled by this paper.

source: Huang et al. (2023/24) Large Language Models Cannot Self-Correct Reasoning Yet
finding: Without an external signal, asking the model to review and revise its own answer does not help and often hurts. With oracle labels telling when to stop, self-correction looks strong, which is an artefact of leaking the answer.
numbers: Intrinsic self-correction, GPT-3.5 (standard / round 1 / round 2): GSM8K 75.9 / 75.1 / 74.7; CommonSenseQA 75.8 / 38.1 / 41.8; HotpotQA 26.0 / 25.0 / 25.0. GPT-4: GSM8K 95.5 / 91.5 / 89.0; CommonSenseQA 82.0 / 79.5 / 80.0; HotpotQA 49.0 / 49.0 / 43.0. With oracle labels GPT-3.5: 84.3 / 89.7 / 29.0; GPT-4: 97.5 / 85.5 / 59.0 (column order GSM8K, CommonSenseQA, HotpotQA). GPT-3.5 keeps its first GSM8K answer 74.7% of the time.
limits: Table cell order was recovered from jumbled PDF text, so the oracle rows are less certain than the intrinsic rows. Two rounds, three benchmarks, prompts from earlier papers.
agent_relevance: Supports G2 and G3: revise from real output, not opinion. Self-evaluated tree search (as in ToT) inherits this weakness when the evaluator is the same model.

source: Lehnert et al. (2024) Beyond A*: Better Planning with Transformers via Search Dynamics Bootstrapping (Searchformer)
finding: A transformer trained on A* execution traces (search dynamics) plans better than one trained on solutions only, and can be bootstrapped to need fewer search steps than A*.
numbers: Sokoban: solves 93.7% of unseen puzzles with on average 26.8% fewer search steps than the A* reference. Search-augmented models reach optimal plans on unseen tasks with 10x fewer training sequences than a larger solution-only model, despite 10x to 100x longer outputs.
limits: Trained from scratch on synthetic maze and Sokoban tasks, not an off-the-shelf LLM. The problems are WSPs with perfect rules. Needs training, which our approach excludes.
agent_relevance: Evidence that writing out the search, not only the answer, is what helps. This supports an explicit visible search record. The scaffold-only analogue is the code-held tree.

source: Long (2023) Large Language Model Guided Tree-of-Thought
finding: A rule-based ToT controller with a checker and a memory of the search history lets the LLM backtrack in Sudoku. It beats zero-shot, one-shot and few-shot prompting on 3x3, 4x4 and 5x5 Sudoku.
numbers: Ten puzzles per size. 3x3: ToT solves all 10. 4x4: failed 1 of 10 within a cap of 100 conversation rounds (9/10), about 80% higher than one-shot and few-shot, which fell to about 0.5. 5x5: failed 2 of 10 (8/10), about 60% higher than one-shot and few-shot.
limits: Ten puzzles per size, no confidence intervals. The rule-based controller cannot tell whether a partial board is completable. Preprint.
agent_relevance: A code-side controller with a checker (our design) beats prompting on fully specified search problems. Backtracking is the missing ingredient.

source: Yao et al. (2023) Tree of Thoughts, related work and framing
finding: The ToT paper links its method to Newell and colleagues' view of problem solving as search. It argues that token-by-token decoding lacks lookahead and backtracking, the two things search provides. It cites Newell, Shaw and Simon (1958 report) and Human Problem Solving (1972).
numbers: No new numbers. The framing quote from Newell et al. appears in the introduction.
limits: A framing claim, not a test. ToT is applied only to tasks with a clear success test (Game of 24, crosswords) or a model-scored task (writing).
agent_relevance: The theory chain from Simon 1973 to ToT to our S6 is explicit, but the LLM work tests WSPs. No study opened here tests the ill-structured case with an external verdict. That gap is our open risk.

source: Gap note: LLM studies of design as ill-structured search (2020-2026)
finding: Within the sources I could open, no LLM study measured search in a truly ill-structured design space with an outside verdict. All measured results are on tasks with a check: Game of 24, crosswords, Sudoku, Blocksworld, HotpotQA, HumanEval. The Semantic Scholar, OpenAlex and arXiv APIs returned rate-limit errors (HTTP 429) so the 2024-2026 design-specific literature was not surveyed in Angle A.
numbers: No numbers. Rate-limited search tools; WebSearch used 5 of 6.
limits: This is a coverage gap, not a finding that none exist. Angle B or C agents should search for LLM design-ideation and design-problem-framing studies.
agent_relevance: The risk for S6 is that its measured benefit comes from tasks with a verifier. Test on a task without one before claiming value for ill-structured problems.
